title: Introduction to Philosophy and Critical Reasoning
summary: Learn the main branches of philosophy, how to build and test arguments, theories of knowledge and ethics, and how to write a clear philosophy essay.
audience: Secondary and university students and anyone who wants to reason better

lessons.title: What philosophy is and how it works

body.p: Philosophy means love of wisdom. It asks basic questions that cannot be settled by an experiment alone: What is real? How do we know? How should we live? What is a just society? Instead of giving answers to memorise, philosophy trains you to think clearly, define words carefully, give reasons and test them against objections.

list: Metaphysics: what exists, and the nature of mind, time and free will.
Epistemology: what knowledge is and how we get it.
Ethics: right and wrong, good and bad.
Political philosophy: justice, rights, power and law.
Logic: the structure of good reasoning.
Aesthetics: beauty and art.

body.p: Philosophy exists in every culture. Examples include Greek thinkers such as Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, Confucius and Laozi in China, the Indian schools, Islamic philosophers such as Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd, and African traditions such as ubuntu, which stresses that a person is a person through other persons.

body.tip: A philosophical answer is a position plus reasons. 'I just feel it' does not count.

body.p: An argument is a set of statements called premises that are offered to support another statement, the conclusion. Not every disagreement is an argument. Shouting is not an argument. A good argument is easy to lay out: P1, P2, therefore C.

An argument is valid if the conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true. It is sound if it is valid and the premises are actually true. Example: P1 All students need to practise. P2 Kemi is a student. C Kemi needs to practise. It is valid and, if the premises are true, sound. Another: P1 All birds can fly. P2 A penguin is a bird. C A penguin can fly. It is valid in form but not sound, because P1 is false.

list: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument.
Straw man: misrepresenting a view to make it easy to attack.
False dilemma: pretending there are only two options.
Appeal to popularity: it must be true because many believe it.
Slippery slope: claiming one step will inevitably lead to extreme results without evidence.
Circular reasoning: the conclusion is already assumed in the premises.

body.tip: To test an argument, try to find a case where the premises are true and the conclusion is false. If you find one, the argument is invalid.

body.p: Epistemology asks what knowledge is. A classic definition says knowledge is justified true belief: you believe it, it is true and you have good reasons. Problems with this view show that luck can break the link between justification and truth, so philosophers keep refining it.

list: Rationalists stress reason: some truths, such as in mathematics, are known by thinking.
Empiricists stress experience: knowledge begins with the senses.
Testimony: we rely on trusted others for most of what we know.
Science combines observation, reasoning and testing, and stays open to correction.

body.p: A sceptic asks how we can be sure that we are not mistaken or dreaming. Descartes doubted everything he could and concluded that the act of thinking proves that he exists. Most philosophers do not think we should stop trusting our senses, but scepticism teaches us to ask for evidence and to be humble about certainty.
Ethics examines right and wrong. Three major approaches give different guides.

list: Consequentialism (such as utilitarianism) judges actions by their results. The right action produces the greatest good for the greatest number.
Deontology judges actions by duties or rules, such as keeping promises and respecting persons, whatever the results.
Virtue ethics asks what a good person would do and stresses character traits such as honesty, courage and fairness.

body.p: A shopkeeper finds that a customer paid too much by mistake. A consequentialist may ask what outcome brings most good, and conclude that returning the money keeps trust in the shop. A deontologist says honesty is a duty, so return it. A virtue ethicist says an honest person would return it. Here all three agree, but they differ in hard cases, such as whether it is ever right to lie to protect someone.

Another view is relativism, which says morality depends on culture. Critics note that it makes it impossible to criticise a harmful practice. Moral philosophy asks us to give reasons, and to treat others with equal concern.

Political philosophy asks why we should obey a state, what a fair society looks like, and what rights people have. Social contract thinkers, such as Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau, suggest that government gets its authority from an agreement among people who give up some freedoms in exchange for order and protection.

Distributive justice concerns how goods are shared. Rawls proposed imagining a veil of ignorance: you design society not knowing your own place in it, so you would choose fair rules in case you were the worst off. Others, such as Nozick, stress property rights and voluntary exchange. Debates continue on equality, merit and need.

list: Negative freedom means freedom from interference.
Positive freedom means having the means to act, such as education and health.
Human rights are claims that all people hold simply by being human, and they are recorded in documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

body.tip: When you discuss a policy, say what value it protects, whom it affects and what an objector would say.

lessons.title: Doing philosophy well: writing, discussion and next steps

body.p: Philosophy is a skill you can practise. To write a short philosophy essay, follow this plan.

steps: State the question and define key terms.
Give your thesis in one sentence.
Set out the best argument for your view as premises and a conclusion.
Present the strongest objection, in a fair form.
Reply to the objection, or adjust your view.

list: Listen to understand before you reply.
Ask for reasons and definitions.
Be willing to change your mind.
Argue against ideas, not people.

body.p: Study of philosophy develops clear writing, logical analysis and ethical judgement, which are valued in law, public policy, journalism, teaching, technology ethics, research and business. Many careers do not list philosophy by name but reward its skills.

body.tip: Keep a notebook of questions that puzzle you. Many good essays begin as a question that will not go away.

quiz.q: Which branch asks what knowledge is?
In an argument, the statement the premises support is called the:

options: The conclusion must be true if the premises are true

quiz.q: 'All birds can fly, a penguin is a bird, so a penguin can fly' is:
Which fallacy attacks the person rather than the argument?
Misrepresenting someone's view so it is easy to attack is the:
The traditional definition of knowledge is:
Empiricists stress that knowledge begins with:
Which approach judges actions by their results?

options: What would a person of good character do

quiz.q: The 'veil of ignorance' is a thought experiment about:
options: Designing fair rules without knowing your place in society

quiz.q: What is the best structure for responding to an objection in an essay?
options: State it fairly and reply to it
